description:
Blazing-fast Claude in your terminal — a C++26 alternative to claude-code.

agentty is a native C++26 terminal coding agent and a drop-in alternative to claude-code. A single static binary with sub-millisecond cold start, sandboxed by default, and one-command SSH air-gap. No Node, Python, or Electron. Signs in with your Claude Pro/Max subscription or an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
Added
- OpenCode Go provider (OPENCODE_API_KEY). It sends the
  x-opencode-session header OpenCode Go now requires, from the first request.
- Every gateway gets its session id the way it wants it. agentty sends a
  stable per-conversation id so routing gateways keep a conversation on one
  backend. The header name now fits the host: your pin, else one learned from
  the host, else the provider's, else x-session-id. A host that refuses a
  request for a "missing x-...-session" header has that name learned and the
  same request resent, so the turn just works, and agentty remembers it. Hosted
  vendors get an opaque id that differs per vendor; your own hosts get the
  thread id. Pin one under "session_headers" in settings.json.
- A subagent's own tool calls show inside its Agent card, one row each
  (icon, tool, detail), newest five with older ones folded into "N earlier".
- ^O on a subagent lists every call it made, then its report as formatted
  prose (headings, bold, code, bullets) instead of numbered raw markdown.
Fixed
- Settings search finds the General toggles such as "Keep retrying on
  errors", and picking one lands on that row (#133).
- The composer no longer bounces while a subagent runs. The Agent card now
  only grows a row at a time.
- Session-header errors no longer say "check the API key".
- Subagents read in parallel. Independent read-only calls in one turn
  (several greps or reads) run side by side instead of one after another.
- The tool panel footer shows the real elapsed time while tools run (it
  read 0ms for a whole agent run), plus the agent's turn when one is
  running: 0/1 action · turn 7/80 1m12s.
- Windows and macOS build again after today's speed work (an MSVC-only
  builtin and a Linux-only sync call).
- Subagents no longer die after doing the work. A reply too long to
  stream (a big write) used to end the whole run at the 8k output limit;
  write-capable agents now get the model's output ceiling (up to 32k), and a
  cut-off turn is retried smaller instead of failing the run.
- A subagent always ends with a report. When it runs out of turns or time
  mid-work, it gets one last turn with no tools to write up what it changed
  or found, instead of returning an activity log.
- Coder subagents start editing. They were spending 40-77 turns reading
  and returning "no edits made"; the coder role now reads narrowly and edits
  early, and every subagent is told its turn and time budget.
- The Agent card got a redesign. While it runs: a budget bar and
  turn 7/80 · 9 tools · 1m 12s pinned above the feed, one line per tool
  call that turns from ○ to ✓ 14.2s or ✗ — why in place, and the
  agent's current sentence last. When it settles: the report with markdown
  cleaned up (no stray **, ## or table pipes), a partial result (out of
  turns or time) in amber with its findings instead of a red "failed", and
  a provider failure explained in a sentence with what to do. A failed run's
  report carries the last dozen steps, not the whole log.
- Live shell output streams again (to the card and to ACP clients); it
  showed only the newest chunk since the background-on-timeout change.
- edit never silently overwrites someone else's change. If the file
  is written by another process between edit's read and its write (a
  formatter on save, your editor), the edit is refused and nothing is lost.
- edit and write keep read-only files read-only and hard links
  linked. The atomic rename replaced a 0444 file straight through its
  permission bit, and split a hard-linked file from its other names.
- A long shell or test call is no longer killed at 330 s. The
  no-progress watchdog now waits for the timeout the call asked for (plus
  slack), so timeout: 600 or timeout_seconds: 1800 runs to its own
  deadline instead of losing its output.
- cd carries over between shell calls inside the sandbox. It was
  saved to a file the sandbox's private /tmp couldn't reach, so every call
  printed "No such file or directory" and the directory never stuck.
- A glob can reach into third_party/, vendor/, build-*/ and the
  like. replace, grep, glob, extract, aggregate and the
  structural tools skipped those directories even when the glob named them,
  and replace just said "No files to scan". An empty scan now says why.
- Globs mean the same thing in every tool: *.{ts,tsx} alternation and
  src/**/*.go paths work in search_structural and rewrite_structural
  too, which only matched file names.
Performance
- edit on large files is ~9x faster (38 ms to 4 ms for a one-line
  edit in a 1 MB, 30,000-line file; 0.4 ms on a typical 2,000-line file).
  Edits splice in place, only the changed region is diffed, and the file is
  diffed once instead of three times.
- edit is ~13x faster (8 ms to 0.6 ms for a one-line edit in a
  2,000-line file): Myers diff instead of a full LCS table, no zero-filled
  multi-megabyte read buffer, and no redundant fdatasync/directory fsync
  when replacing an existing file on btrfs or ext4, which already order the
  data before the rename.
- Sandboxed shell is ~45% faster (22 ms to 12 ms for true). It no
  longer forks a fresh host probe per command, re-walks the workspace for
  the secret mask (an inotify watch answers "nothing changed"), binds
  missing optional paths, watches git's .sample hooks, or re-sorts the
  seccomp table on every insert.
- grep is ~40% faster (32 ms to 19 ms on this repo), from the same
  spawn savings.
